name: Groundswell // Drowned City Tour Tee
description:
Black short-sleeve tee in a slightly heavier-than-average cotton-synth blend, with a screen-printed design on the chest: a stylized skyline half-submerged in abstract water, rendered in white and electric teal. On the back, a list of cities and dates from the 2197 Drowned City tour — including two that were cancelled mid-run after a venue shutdown in the southern arc. The print has a slightly cracked, worn texture even on new shirts, which is either an aesthetic choice or a cost-cutting measure depending on who you ask.

Groundswell is a noise-ambient band out of the lower Shelf, known for shows that run too long, sound systems that border on damaging, and lyrics that are more felt than understood. The tour tee has become something of a marker in certain circles — people who were actually at the shows wear them differently than people who bought them after. Both groups exist, and both are legitimate.
what_it_says: You were there — or you wish you were, which is almost the same thing. Either way, you know the name.
worn_by: people who find them at secondhand stalls
anyone who likes the image without knowing the band
story_hooks: The two cancelled shows are rumored to have been shut down by Vantablack contractors — what was said on stage that night that warranted it?
A run of counterfeit Drowned City tees is circulating, slightly wrong in ways that only the faithful notice — and someone's using the fakes to identify who's paying close attention.
The lead singer of Groundswell disappeared three months after the tour ended. The shirt is the last piece of merch from before.

physical_description.visual_profile: A slightly oversized, lived-in black tee with a haunting chest print: a half-drowned cityscape in white and electric teal that seems to shift between data corruption and genuine drowning. The back lists tour dates in small, industrial lettering. Worn with casual authority by people who either survived the shows or wish they had.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, slightly boxy through the shoulders and torso. Not fitted but not baggy—designed to sit comfortably over baseline humans and light augmentation. Sleeves hit mid-bicep with a gentle roll.
physical_description.primary_material: Cotton-synthetic blend, heavier weight than standard merch tees. Approximately 60% organic cotton, 40% performance synth to justify the durability claim.
physical_description.texture: Soft but substantial. The screen-printed design has a deliberate cracked, aged texture—intentional distressing that reads as either artistic or economical depending on context. Print feels slightly raised and granular under fingertips.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep black base with stark white print accents and electric teal highlights on the skyline. The teal glows faintly under certain light angles, hinting at phosphorescent treatment in the ink.
physical_description.closures: None—simple crew neck, no collar. No tags visible on most worn examples; they're usually removed or worn away.
distinctive_features: Screen-printed skyline showing half-submerged buildings with abstract wave forms
Back print: full tour roster with two visibly struck-through venue names (bootleg history)
Deliberate print cracking that ages the garment aesthetically
Slight sheen variation suggesting uneven ink application or intentional patina
No visible brand marking beyond the design itself—pure band identity
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3-4 crossover. Cheap enough to acquire at shows (≈45 Φ), but worn by people across socioeconomic strata who care more about subcultural credentials than wealth signaling.
physical_description.cultural_context: Anti-corpo music scene. Post-capitalist aesthetic without the irony. Worn by noise enthusiasts, venue workers, people living in the flooded districts, and data-anarchists. The shirt is proof of experience or aspiration toward experience—both are currency in lower Shelf circles.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in from day one due to the pre-cracked print. Edges of print fray naturally. Most examples show armpit staining, faded teal, and subtle wear on the collar and cuffs. Looks better worn than new.
